chartTable.do2: Place both in a titled card — a complete report block.
chartTable.dont1: Placing the chart and table in two separate spots, forcing viewers to scroll back and forth to compare.
chartTable.exHorizD: Wide screen: chart on the left, detail table on the right — glance at the shape then read the figures right beside it.
chartTable.exVertT: Chart + Table — In a card, stacked
chartTable.exVertD: A compact report block: title, chart, then the data table — reusable across many pages.
chartTable.title: Chart + Table

sparkline.desc: A shrunken trend line, no axes or labels — fits inside a table cell or the corner of a metric card to show direction at a glance.
sparkline.purpose: Answer 'trending up or down?' in a very small space — a complement to the main number.
sparkline.behavior: Auto-scales to the data's min–max; only the shape, no axes/labels. Leave detailed figures to a dedicated report screen.
sparkline.avoid: When viewers need to read the VALUE of each point — use a full bar/line chart.
sparkline.when1: The corner of a KPI card on a dashboard
sparkline.when2: A "trend" column in a department table
sparkline.when3: Beside a total figure in a summary sentence
sparkline.do1: Always place it beside a main number (KPI card, table cell) — the sparkline is only context.
sparkline.do2: For a good upward trend use the primary/green color; for a bad trend switch to red to warn.
sparkline.dont1: Using it in place of a report chart — without axes you can't compare precisely.
sparkline.exLineD: line is stroke only; area also fills below the line (15% color) — stands out more on a wide card.
sparkline.exColorD: Change color by direction: green for growth, red for a declining series to catch the eye.
sparkline.exInlineD: A tiny 80×20 size fits neatly inside a sentence or a table cell beside the number.
sparkline.title: Sparkline

tracker.desc: Each square is a day/shift/run — skim one strip to read the whole status streak: monthly attendance, an on-time streak.
tracker.purpose: Compress 20–31 sequential statuses into a small strip to see the overall 'rhythm' without a table.
tracker.behavior: Each cell is colored by status; hover a cell to show the date + status detail. A gray cell = not counted (weekend, not yet reached).
tracker.avoid: Data with no time sequence — use a Category Bar or a table.
tracker.when2: A streak of on-time report submissions
tracker.do1: Keep a fixed system-wide palette: green met, amber needs attention, red violation, gray not counted.
tracker.do2: Always include a per-cell tooltip — the strip only gives an overall sense, detail lives in the tooltip.
tracker.dont1: Cramming more than 31 cells into one strip — if too long, split by month.
tracker.exMonthD: One employee's 30 days: green present, amber late, red unexcused absence, gray weekend. Hover a cell to see the specific day.
tracker.exTeamD: One row per employee — compare the whole team's attendance rhythm in one small block.
tracker.exSizeD: Adjust cellW/cellH/gap to fit the space: large cells for a standalone block, small cells to fit a table row.
tracker.title: Tracker

barList.desc: One item per row: label + proportion bar + number — quickly compare top departments or branches on a dashboard.
barList.purpose: Answer 'who's the most, and by how much?' for a short ranked list.
barList.behavior: The longest bar = the largest value, other bars scale proportionally. The label sits INSIDE the bar, the number right-aligned in a column.
barList.avoid: More than 8–10 items or when a precise axis/unit is needed — use a full bar chart or a table.
barList.when2: Comparing branches by a single metric
barList.do1: Sort data descending before passing it in — a ranking is read top to bottom.
barList.do2: Keep one color for the whole list; only recolor an item that needs a warning.
barList.dont1: Mixing two metrics with different units into one list.
barList.exHeadcountD: Top departments by headcount — label inside the bar, number on the right.
barList.exHighlightT: Bar List — Highlight an item to watch
barList.exHighlightD: Recolor an item that crosses a threshold (unusually high overtime hours) to draw the eye to the right spot.
barList.title: Bar List

categoryBar.desc: ONE horizontal bar split into proportional segments with a legend — headcount composition, contract-type distribution, more compact than a pie chart.
categoryBar.purpose: Show 'what parts make up this total, and which dominates' in the space of a single row.
categoryBar.behavior: Segments split proportionally on ONE bar; the legend below shows the label + an auto-computed %. Default colors come from the data palette, cycling.
categoryBar.avoid: More than 5–6 segments or a segment too small (<3%) — merge into 'Other' before passing it in.
categoryBar.when2: Distribution of request statuses in a period
categoryBar.do1: Put the largest segment first — the eye reads left to right.
categoryBar.do2: Merge minor segments into 'Other' so the bar isn't fragmented.
categoryBar.dont1: Using it when you need to compare nearly equal segments PRECISELY — a data table does that better.
categoryBar.exContractD: Headcount composition by contract type — largest segment first, % auto-computed from raw values.
categoryBar.exColorD: Assign semantic colors when a segment carries a status meaning: approved (green), pending (amber), rejected (red).
categoryBar.exNoLegendD: Turn off the legend when placed in a tight table cell — the bar still conveys the proportions.
categoryBar.title: Category Bar

orgChart.desc: An org tree of people: card-style nodes (avatar + job title + department), direct report lines (solid) and indirect/matrix reports (dashed). View vertically/horizontally, compact, collapse-expand each branch, drag-pan and zoom.
orgChart.ovHint: click a node to highlight its reporting line up to the top, click again to deselect. Drag the background to move, scroll to zoom.
orgChart.purpose: Present an organization's reporting structure: who manages whom, nested departments, indirect (matrix) reporting relationships.
orgChart.behavior: A node = a person card; solid line = direct report; dashed line = indirect report. The toolbar changes orientation (vertical/horizontal), compact, expand/collapse all, zoom. Clicking a node emits selectedId + nodeClick. Text in a node is caller-supplied data; button labels come via [labels] (i18n).
orgChart.avoid: A tree too deep/wide shown all at once — collapse branches or select a sub-root to focus.
orgChart.when2: Viewing direct and matrix reporting lines
orgChart.do1: Use a distinct dashed line for indirect (matrix) reports to separate them from the main reporting line.
orgChart.do2: Collapse deep branches; let viewers expand them when needed.
orgChart.do3: Give a badge with the number of reports to quickly grasp each branch's size.
orgChart.dont1: Cramming too many lines of text into one node — keep name + job title + 1 supporting line.
orgChart.exHorizD: Set [orientation]='horizontal' (or click the Horizontal button on the toolbar). Suits deep reporting trees with few horizontal branches.
orgChart.exMatrixT: Org Chart — Indirect (matrix) reports + reporting-line highlight
orgChart.exMatrixD: dottedReports draws a dashed line to a secondary report node (Recruitment Specialist ↔ CTO). [highlightPath]='true' → clicking one node dims the rest and highlights the reporting line to the root.
orgChart.exSearchD: [searchable] type a name/title → highlight + center (‹ › to step through results). [showCounts] shows the total reports beneath. [focusable] double-click a node to view that branch alone, the Home button returns to the root.
orgChart.exCompactD: [compact]='true' makes nodes small; [showToolbar]='false' hides the toolbar when embedding in a dashboard.
orgChart.title: Org chart

orgChartTpl.title: Org Chart
orgChartTpl.desc: Org-chart screen template: page header + the Design System's hrm-org-chart component filling the frame — with view modes / search / collapse / zoom. No hand-drawn tree.
orgChartTpl.purpose: A company-wide org-chart screen by department / position / employee — built quickly from the existing hrm-org-chart component.
orgChartTpl.when1: The “Org Chart” screen in the HR module
orgChartTpl.when2: View the reporting tree and headcount per unit
orgChartTpl.when3: Quickly look up a person's position / department
orgChartTpl.behavior: Uses hrm-org-chart directly: switch view mode, search, focus a branch, collapse/expand, drag-pan, zoom. Frame height is set via the --org-height variable.
orgChartTpl.avoid: Don't hand-roll the tree in HTML/CSS — a standard component already exists in the Design System.
orgChartTpl.do1: Use hrm-org-chart with [data] as an HrmOrgNode tree and i18n [labels].
orgChartTpl.do2: Set --org-height so the chart fills the screen content area.
orgChartTpl.do3: Default to Department mode for the “Org Chart” screen.
orgChartTpl.dont1: Do not embed a hand-drawn chart outside the Design System.

alert.desc: An in-content notice block: info, success, warning, error — stays visible until the user acts on it.
alert.ovDesc: The system will be down on Sunday, from 2 AM to 4 AM.
alert.purpose: Tell the user about a situation right in the page — form errors, system updates, maintenance notices, or a success confirmation.
alert.behavior: Color and icon change automatically by type. The notice stays until the user reads and handles it; it can be closable or carry an action button.
alert.avoid: A transient notice that disappears on its own after a few seconds — use Message.
alert.when1: Show a form-level error summary before submitting
alert.when3: Confirm an action that just completed
alert.do1: Pick the type that matches the content: info for updates, warning for caution, error for problems, success for confirmation.
alert.do2: Make info and success notices closable; keep error notices visible until the user has fixed the issue.
alert.do3: Keep titles short and scannable: "Approval failed" instead of "Something went wrong while processing your request".
alert.dont1: Use it for a notice that self-dismisses after a few seconds — use Message.
alert.dont2: Stack several notices of the same type — merge them into one.
alert.exStatusD: Four types: info, success, warning, error. Use them to show notices that must persist — updates, confirmations, cautions or problems — at the top of a page or a section.
alert.st1Desc: You can start your self-assessment today.
alert.st2Desc: Your manager will receive your request right away.
alert.st3Desc: Please add your ID number before signing the contract.
alert.st4Desc: Cannot approve because a higher-level approver is missing.
alert.exActionD: Add a button to the notice so the user can act right there. Use it for contracts about to expire, timekeeping errors, or anything that needs a response.
alert.acDesc: Your contract will expire in 7 days.
alert.exCloseD: Let the user close the notice once they have read it. Use it for maintenance notices, feature tips, or any low-priority reminder the user can acknowledge and dismiss.
alert.clDesc: Tap a day to see check-in/out details.
alert.exBannerD: A notice banner that spans the full width with no rounded corners, used at the top of a page for system-wide announcements or maintenance schedules.
alert.bn1Msg: The system will be under maintenance on Sunday, 2 AM–4 AM.
alert.bn2Msg: This month's timekeeping deadline is the 25th — please clear the remaining requests.
alert.exSoftD: Floating notification cards: an icon in a rounded square, a bold title with a one-line subtitle. Five tones: neutral, blue, success, warning, error. For toasts and lightweight alerts.
alert.sf2Desc: Tap the bell to see the latest updates.
alert.sf3Desc: Your August timesheet was sent for approval.
alert.sf4Desc: 2 days left to finish this month's attendance.
alert.sf5Desc: Lost connection to the server — please try again.
alert.title: Alert

progress.desc: A horizontal bar showing how many percent of a task is complete — file uploads, payroll processing, data syncs.
progress.purpose: Show the user how many percent of a task has run, or indicate processing when progress cannot yet be measured.
progress.behavior: The bar grows with the percentage and shows the % at the end. Color changes by context: blue while running, green when done, red on error.
progress.avoid: Instant tasks (done on click) — no progress bar needed; or fully unmeasurable tasks — use Spin.
progress.when1: File upload / download with a percentage
progress.do1: Use a % bar when the total workload is known (uploading 10 files, processing 500 rows); show "processing" when it is not.
progress.do2: Pick a color to match the context: blue for general progress, green when complete, red on error.
progress.do3: Put a label next to the bar describing what is happening ("Loading payroll…") so the user knows what they are waiting for.
progress.dont1: Cram text or icons inside the bar — keep the label outside for a clean, readable layout.
progress.dont2: Stack several bars for the same task — use a single bar with a % value.
progress.exStatusD: Four states: normal, active, success (green), exception (red). Color tells the user right away whether things are fine or something is wrong.
progress.exLabelD: Show or hide the % at the end of the bar. Show the number when the user needs an exact value; hide it when a quick sense of the level is enough.
progress.exTypeD: Line for lists and forms; circle and dashboard for stat cards or dashboards where progress is a standout number.
progress.exStepsD: Split the bar into separate segments to count steps or completed items — for example 4 of 5 HR profiles approved.
progress.exSizeD: Small for dense UI (table rows, compact cards); default for a primary area where progress needs to be clearly visible.
progress.title: Progress

spin.desc: A spinning icon indicating the system is loading or processing something with an unpredictable duration.
spin.purpose: Tell the user the system is busy and to wait — use it when loading data or submitting a form, where the wait time is unpredictable.
spin.behavior: The icon spins continuously until done. It can stand alone, carry a descriptive label, or overlay the content block being loaded.
spin.avoid: A content area whose size is already known — use Skeleton to preserve the layout instead of covering it with a spinner.
spin.when3: A short task with no measurable % progress
spin.do1: Add a descriptive label of what is loading ("Loading the employee list…") so users and screen readers understand.
spin.do2: On a dark or strong-colored background, switch the spinner to a light color so it stays visible.
spin.do3: Each screen should have only one spinner representing the overall loading state.
spin.dont1: Use it for an area of known size — use Skeleton so the layout does not jump.
spin.dont2: Place several spinners at once in one view — it is cluttered and unclear what is being awaited.
spin.exSizeD: Three sizes — small, medium, large — side by side. Small for buttons or table rows, medium for most cases, large when overlaying a whole page.
spin.exLabelD: A spinner with text telling what is loading. Stating the running task reassures users while they wait and supports screen readers.
spin.rowLabelLong: long label, describing the task clearly
spin.tipLong: Loading the Accounting department employee list…
spin.exMediaD: On a dark or strong-colored background, switch the spinner to a light color so it stays prominent — use it on cover images, banners or color accent blocks.
spin.exOverlayD: The spinner overlays the block being loaded (card, list) — the user still sees the content frame while waiting for data.
spin.title: Spin

skeleton.desc: Shimmering gray blocks mimicking the shape of the content while waiting for data.
skeleton.exBasicD: The default placeholder has one title line and a few content lines, replaced by real data once loaded.
skeleton.purpose: Show the user the shape of the loading content in advance, reducing the sense of waiting and impatience.
skeleton.behavior: Shows shimmering gray blocks matching the real layout (image, title, text lines). When data arrives, the gray blocks are replaced by real content.
skeleton.avoid: The content size/layout is unknown in advance, or the wait is very short — use a Spinner instead.
skeleton.when1: Loading a page or card with a clear layout
skeleton.when2: A list/table loading for the first time
skeleton.when3: An employee profile card waiting for data
skeleton.do1: Draw a placeholder that matches the size and shape of the incoming content so the eye does not jump on the swap.
skeleton.do2: For lists, repeat a few identical placeholders to signal several rows are loading.
skeleton.dont1: Use it when the content layout is unclear — use a Spinner instead of a placeholder.
skeleton.dont2: Let the placeholder run forever — if loading takes too long, switch to an error or empty state.
skeleton.exTextD: A placeholder of text lines only, no image. Use it for descriptions, notes, or text content being loaded.
skeleton.exCardD: A card placeholder with an avatar, name and a few info lines. Use it while loading an employee profile card.
skeleton.exListD: Repeat several identical placeholders when loading an employee list for the first time, each row with an image and two text lines.
skeleton.exTableD: Compact placeholder rows (no title, single line) when a timekeeping or payroll table loads row by row.
skeleton.title: Skeleton

result.desc: A screen reporting the final result of a large operation: an icon, title, description and a button for the next step.
result.ovSub: The request has been sent to your direct manager and is awaiting approval.
result.purpose: Report the final result of a large flow (submitting a request, closing timekeeping, filing a profile) and point out the next step.
result.behavior: Shows a large status icon + title + short description, with 1–2 buttons guiding the user onward.
result.avoid: A small, instant response after a single action (save, copy) — use Message or Toast.
result.when1: The end screen of a large flow (submitting a request, closing timekeeping, filing a profile)
result.when3: Confirming an important action has completed
result.do1: Always have a clear title and at least one button for the next step, so the user does not get "stuck" on the result screen.
result.do2: Pick the correct semantic status: green when done, red when failed, amber when caution is needed — not for decoration.
result.do3: Say specifically what happened ("The request was sent to your manager") rather than something generic ("Completed").
result.dont1: Use Result for a small form error that needs fixing in place — reporting the error right below the field fits better.
result.dont2: Leave the result screen completely empty with no button — the user has nowhere to go next.
result.exActionD: A done or failed status with a button for the next step: go home, review the request, or retry. The button helps the user move on instead of stopping at the notice.
result.ac1Sub: The profile has been saved to the system; HR will review it within 1–2 days.
result.ac2Sub: Lost connection to the server. Please check your network and try submitting again.
result.exStatusD: Four semantic states: done, failed, caution, info. Pick the correct icon color so the user grasps the result at a glance before reading any text.
result.st1Sub: The June timesheet is locked and can no longer be edited.
result.st2Sub: 3 employees are missing a bank account number.
result.st3Sub: 5 leave requests are overdue for approval and need handling before the weekend.
result.st4Sub: The Q3 review round starts on 01/07.
result.exAccessD: A 403 screen when the user lacks permission and 404 when the page does not exist. Always include a back button so they can leave the dead end cleanly.
result.e403Title: You do not have permission to view this page
result.e403Sub: The payroll page is for HR only. Contact an administrator if you need access.
result.e404Sub: The profile may have been deleted or moved to another unit.
result.exServerD: A 500 screen when the server hits a problem beyond the user's control. Reassure them the error is not their fault and offer a retry button or a way to report it to the technical team.
result.e500Title: The system is experiencing an issue
result.e500Sub: This is not your fault. We are fixing it; please try again in a few minutes.
result.title: Result

modal.desc: A window floating in the center of the screen that dims and blocks the background, forcing the user to decide before continuing.
modal.ovInfoContent: The leave request has been sent to your manager.
modal.purpose: Show an overlay that blocks interaction with the page until the user responds — for delete confirmations, quick forms, accepting terms, or decisions that should not be skipped.
modal.behavior: Floats in the center and dims the background. Depending on purpose, it can close via a button, the Esc key, or a click on the backdrop; a required dialog only closes when an action is chosen.
modal.avoid: A simple notice that could show right in the page or as a toast — do not interrupt with a modal.
modal.when1: Confirming an important or dangerous action
modal.when2: Quickly filling a short form without leaving the page
modal.when3: Requiring acceptance of terms before continuing
modal.do1: Pick the right level of blocking: info for read-and-dismiss content, form to avoid losing data on an accidental backdrop click, required when a choice is mandatory.
modal.do2: Always have a clear title at the top so the user immediately understands what the dialog is asking.
modal.do3: Keep the dialog focused on one task; if the content grows beyond the frame, move it to a dedicated page.
modal.dont1: Use a dialog for a simple notice that should show right in the page or as a toast.
modal.dont2: Nest a dialog inside a dialog — split the flow into steps within the same dialog.
modal.exConfirmD: Ask again before an action that cannot be undone. Use it when deleting an employee profile, removing a member from a department, or canceling a contract — the delete button is red as a warning.
modal.cfContent: This will permanently delete the profile "Nguyen Van A" and all related data. This cannot be undone.
modal.exNotifyD: A dialog just to report a result; click to close once read. Use it for a saved confirmation, a reminder, or short info that needs no choice from the user.
modal.nfInfoContent: The leave request has been forwarded to your direct manager for approval.
modal.nfSuccessContent: The June timesheet has been closed.
modal.nfWarningContent: Contracts of 3 employees will expire this week.
modal.exFormD: Enter information right in the dialog without leaving the page. A backdrop click does not close it, to avoid accidentally losing what you are typing — fits editing a profile or adding a note.
modal.phNote: Additional details about the emergency contact…
modal.exRequiredD: Cannot be closed with the Esc key or a backdrop click; the user must choose an action. Use it for work handovers, accepting terms, or important decisions that must not be skipped.
modal.rqBody: You are about to hand over all the work you are responsible for to someone else. After you confirm, your edit rights on these items will be revoked. Please choose an action to continue.
modal.exSizeD: Small for a compact confirmation, medium for a form, fullscreen for content needing more space like an editor or a long table.
modal.szBody: Sample content to illustrate the dialog width. Pick a width that matches the amount of information inside — a dialog too wide for short content looks empty.
modal.exScrollD: Cap the height and let the dialog body scroll when the content is long. Use it for terms, regulations, or change history — things the user needs to review before agreeing.
modal.clauseBody: Employees are responsible for complying with the labor rules, working hours and safety regulations issued. Any change to shifts, leave or business trips must be registered and approved following the HR department's proper procedure.
modal.title: Modal

message.desc: A small notice that briefly appears at the top center of the screen, confirms an action, then disappears on its own.
message.purpose: Tell the user what just happened right after an action (saved, deleted, sent) — a response is needed, not a decision.
message.behavior: Appears briefly at the top center then hides after a few seconds; it does not block interaction and needs no close click. Error messages should stay longer.
message.avoid: Important information that must be read, or an error that halts work — use Alert or Notification.
message.when1: A quick confirmation after saving / deleting / sending
message.when2: Reporting that an action just succeeded or failed
message.when3: A short note that needs no response from the user
message.do1: Keep it very short, just a few words stating what happened: "Saved", "Request sent".
message.do2: Use the error type for failures that need attention; keep it longer so the user does not miss it.
message.do3: For a slow action, show "processing" first, then switch to the result when done.
message.dont1: Cram in long, multi-line content — the message self-dismisses after a few seconds and the reader cannot keep up.
message.dont2: Report a form input error with Message — report it right at the field so the user knows what to fix.
message.exTypesD: Four types by tone: success, error, info, warning. Color and icon make the nature obvious without careful reading.
message.tErrorMsg: Could not send the request, try again
message.exLoadingD: A long-running task (exporting a report, syncing) shows 'processing' held on screen, then switches to a result notice when done.
message.exStackD: Several messages at once stack neatly in order, with newer ones pushed below. Click multiple times to see how they appear and dismiss one by one.
message.stMsg1: Approved the request from Nguyen Van A
message.stMsg2: Approved the request from Tran Thi B
message.stMsg3: Approved the request from Le Van C
message.exDurationD: Choose a long or short duration by importance: ordinary confirmations dismiss quickly, while errors stay longer so the user can read them.
message.title: Message

notification.desc: A notice box in a corner of the screen, with a title and content, that stays longer so the user can read it.
notification.ovSuccessDesc: The leave request has been approved
notification.purpose: Report an event with content longer than one line, which the user should notice but need not stop to decide on.
notification.behavior: Appears in a corner of the screen with a title and description; stays a while then closes on its own, or lets the user close it. Multiple notices stack in order.
notification.avoid: A very short response (Saved) — use Message. An error that needs confirmation before moving on — use Dialog.
notification.when1: Report new work to handle (requests awaiting approval, contracts expiring soon)
notification.when2: Completing a background task (exporting a report, syncing data)
notification.when3: A system error that needs attention but does not block interaction
notification.do1: Keep the content concise: one title and one description sentence, enough to grasp what just happened.
notification.do2: Use the error type for failures that need attention — keep it until the user closes it so nothing is missed.
notification.do3: Deduplicate with a key when an action repeats many times (clicking sync repeatedly) to avoid spam.
notification.dont1: Fire too many notices at once and create noise — batch them or use a dedup key.
notification.dont2: Cram in long, multi-line content — the notice closes on its own and the user may not finish reading.
notification.dont3: Show a form input error with a notification — report the error right at the field so the user knows where to fix it.
notification.exTypesD: Four semantic types: info, success, warning, error. Different colors and icons make the nature of the event recognizable right away.
notification.tInfoDesc: There are 3 leave requests awaiting your approval
notification.tSuccessDesc: Tran Van B's leave request has been approved
notification.tWarningDesc: Contracts of 2 employees expire this week
notification.tErrorDesc: Could not sync data from the timekeeping device
notification.exPlaceD: Appears in one of the four screen corners. Top right is the default; change the corner when you need to avoid covering the content in use.
notification.exDurationD: Auto-close after a few seconds for light news; keep it (no auto-close) for important things like errors, forcing the user to close it once read.
notification.durAutoDesc: The June payroll has been saved as a draft
notification.durStayDesc: 5 timesheets are missing data, please check again
notification.exDedupD: With the same key, a new notice overwrites the old one instead of stacking. Use it when an action repeats continuously — for example HR sync progress.
notification.exStackD: Several notices shown at once stack in order, with newer ones on top. Click to see them appear one by one then close on their own.
notification.stMsg1Desc: Nguyen Van A was just added to the Engineering department
notification.stMsg2Desc: Le Thi C's business trip request has been approved
notification.stMsg3Desc: 4 timesheets are not closed before 5 PM
notification.title: Notification

menu.title: Menu
menu.desc: A list of navigation items — laid out horizontally as a bar, or vertically with sub-groups — to switch between areas within a page.
menu.purpose: Let users switch between areas/functions inside a single page or HR module.
menu.behavior: The selected item gets a light background (pill). Items with a sub-group expand on click; a horizontal menu opens the sub-group as a dropdown, a vertical menu expands it right below.
menu.avoid: This is NOT the main navigation bar for the whole application — use the Side Nav (Appshell) for the app-wide left rail. This menu is for local navigation within content.
menu.when1: Local navigation within a page/module (not the app-wide left rail)
menu.when2: A horizontal bar of top-level areas at the top of a page
menu.when3: A vertical menu grouping items by function
menu.do1: Clearly mark the selected item so users always know where they are.
menu.do2: Gather related items into a titled sub-group (submenu) — e.g. "People" holds Recruitment, Attendance.
menu.do3: Use a horizontal menu for a few top-level items; a vertical menu when there are multi-level sub-groups.
menu.dont1: Nesting the menu too deep — hrm-menu supports only one sub-group level; anything deeper is hard to find.
menu.dont2: Using this menu in place of the app-wide Side Nav — they play different roles; avoid duplicating navigation.
menu.exHorizD: Lay out HR modules/areas in a single horizontal row. Use it at the top of an overview page or below a module title, when there are only a few top-level items and no sub-groups are needed.
menu.exVertD: A vertical (inline) menu with an expandable sub-group: 'People' holds Recruitment and Attendance. Use it for a local navigation rail on the left of a configuration or detail page.
menu.exGroupsD: Several parallel sub-groups, each with its own title, using submenus to partition the areas. Well suited to an HR settings page with many items: Organization, Compensation, System.
menu.exCollapseD: Left: the same menu collapsed to make room for content — labels hidden, only a narrow strip remains. Right: an item locked (disabled) when the user lacks permission or has not reached that step yet.

dropdown.title: Dropdown
dropdown.desc: A hidden menu that opens on a button click to pick an action: Edit, Duplicate, Delete…
dropdown.purpose: Gather several actions for a row/item into one button that opens a list on demand — keeping the interface compact.
dropdown.behavior: Click the button to reveal the action list; picking an item closes the menu. The delete action is colored red as a warning.
dropdown.avoid: Using it as a menu to navigate between pages — use a navigation bar for that.
dropdown.when2: An account or options menu in the top bar
dropdown.when3: Several secondary actions that need tucking away to stay tidy
dropdown.do1: Keep item names short, starting with a verb (Edit, Duplicate, Export) for fast scanning.
dropdown.do2: Use dividers and titled groups to separate action groups when the menu has many items.
dropdown.do3: Color destructive actions like Delete red (danger) and set them apart.
dropdown.dont1: Cramming more than 10–12 items into one flat menu without grouping.
dropdown.dont2: Hiding the primary action (Save) inside a dropdown.
dropdown.exActionsD: A row's action menu, using a divider to separate safe actions (Edit, Duplicate) from the destructive one (Delete). Use it for actions on an employee, contract or document row.
dropdown.exIconD: Each item carries a leading icon to speed up action recognition when scanning. Use it when the menu has many easily confused items.
dropdown.exOverflowD: A button with only a three-dot icon, no text — saving space for actions on a table row, card or list item. This is the familiar 'more actions' menu on each row.
dropdown.exSectionsD: Items arranged into titled groups for easy scanning. Use it when the menu has many actions belonging to different groups, for example Create and Manage.
dropdown.exDisabledD: Some items are dimmed when the user lacks permission, for example admin-only actions. The user still sees that the action exists but cannot click it.
dropdown.exTriggerD: Choose to open the menu by clicking or by hovering. Click suits table actions (no accidental pop-ups when passing over); hover suits an account/options menu in the top bar.

breadcrumb.title: Breadcrumb
breadcrumb.desc: Shows the current page's position in the structure and lets users go back up to higher levels.
breadcrumb.purpose: Tell users where they are in the system and let them jump back to a parent level quickly.
breadcrumb.behavior: Shows a chain of links from the root page to the current page; click an earlier level to go back. The last level is the current page, so it is plain text, not a link.
breadcrumb.avoid: A flat, single-level page with no hierarchy — a breadcrumb there only adds clutter.
breadcrumb.when1: A detail screen nested several levels deep
breadcrumb.when2: Needing to jump back to a parent level quickly
breadcrumb.when3: A settings panel or configuration page
breadcrumb.do1: Place the breadcrumb right above the page title so users see their location before reading the content.
breadcrumb.do2: Keep labels short and matching the name of the page they link to — "Attendance" instead of "Attendance management page".
breadcrumb.do3: Leave the last level as plain text (not a link) because it is the page being viewed.
breadcrumb.dont1: Using a breadcrumb in place of the main navigation bar — it only complements the side menu, it does not replace it.
breadcrumb.dont2: Letting the chain run longer than 5 levels; if you need more, restructure the pages to be tidier.
breadcrumb.exBasicD: A chain of links from the root page to the current page. The last level is the page being viewed, so it is plain text; earlier levels are clickable to go back.
breadcrumb.exIconsD: Add an icon before the label for quick recognition — a home icon for the root page and contextual icons for important items.
breadcrumb.exSepD: Swap the default slash for another character such as an arrow or a dot when the page style calls for a distinct separator.
breadcrumb.exDeepD: A five-level chain for deeply nested content — like an employee profile inside a department and branch. Try not to exceed five levels.

steps.title: Steps
steps.desc: Shows progress through the multiple steps of a process.
steps.purpose: Show users which step of a multi-step process they are on and how many steps remain.
steps.behavior: Completed, current and upcoming steps are clearly distinguished by color and icon. An errored step is marked so users know where to act.
steps.avoid: A single-step process, or steps that have no fixed order.
steps.when3: An approval flow across several levels
steps.do1: Keep step names short, following the actual order of the process.
steps.do2: Always highlight the current step so users know where they are.
steps.do3: Use the vertical layout when each step needs a long description or the screen is narrow.
steps.dont1: Using it for a simple single-step action — redundant and cluttering.
steps.exProcD: The steps for taking on a new employee, highlighting the step in progress. The owner knows how far the candidate has gotten.
steps.exVertD: Lay the steps out vertically with a description for each step. Suits a narrow screen or when each step needs extra explanation.
steps.exDotD: A minimal style using dots instead of numbers. Suits when you only need to hint at progress without taking up much space.
steps.exDotRow: Currently at the Sign contract step
steps.exErrD: Mark a step red when it hits a problem midway — for example an invalid profile. Users see immediately where to act.

stepper.title: Stepper
stepper.desc: A step-navigation bar for multi-step forms: completed steps get a tick, and you can click back to an earlier step — unlike Steps, which only displays progress.
stepper.purpose: Break a long form into smaller steps and let users know where they are and which step they can go back to.
stepper.behavior: Completed = green tick; current = bold outline; later steps dimmed. You can click BACK to a completed step (by default), but not skip forward past an unfinished one — the Next button lets the form validate and then advance the step.
stepper.avoid: Only needing to DISPLAY processing progress (no navigation) — use Steps.
stepper.when3: Setting up a review cycle across several small screens
stepper.do1: 3–5 steps is about right; beyond that, merge steps.
stepper.do2: Validate on the form's "Next" button; do not allow free jumping between steps.
stepper.dont1: Using it as a single status indicator (approved/processing) — that is the job of Steps/Status.
stepper.exWizardD: 3 steps: pick type → fill details → confirm. The Next/Back buttons drive the steps; click a completed step to go back.
stepper.exVertD: The vertical style shows a description under each step — suits the left panel of a long form.
stepper.exDotD: Dots only — for a compact header or narrow screen, when the step labels already appear elsewhere.
stepper.stTypeDesc: Pick a leave type: annual, unpaid, sick…
stepper.stInfoDesc: Fill in the leave dates, reason and handover person.
stepper.stConfirmDesc: Review everything and send to your manager for approval.

tabs.title: Tabs
tabs.desc: Split content into multiple tabs, viewing one part at a time on the same screen.
tabs.purpose: Gather several groups of content onto one screen; users switch tabs to view each part.
tabs.behavior: Only one tab shows at a time; click a tab title to switch. The selected tab is highlighted.
tabs.avoid: Content that needs to be seen at once for comparison — place it side by side rather than hiding it in tabs.
tabs.when1: A detail screen with several content groups (info/contract/history)
tabs.when2: Splitting a settings page into several sections
tabs.when3: Gathering a multi-faceted report onto one screen
tabs.do1: Use it for a detail screen with several groups (info / contract / history).
tabs.do2: Put the most important tab first and open it by default on entry.
tabs.do3: Keep tab titles short; add an icon when you want quick recognition.
tabs.dont1: Hiding important information that must be seen right away in a secondary tab.
tabs.exIconD: The selected tab uses a filled, accent-colored icon; unselected tabs use a thin, gray icon. Users recognize instantly which part they are on.
tabs.exBasicD: A simple tab set with text titles and separate content for each tab. Use it for most detail screens in HRM.
tabs.exSizeD: Small, medium, large. Small for dense areas, medium for most screens, large for a prominent detail page.
tabs.exTypeD: The underline style is light for in-page content; the card style reads as a more distinct block, suiting tabs that are the main area of the screen.

pagination.title: Pagination
pagination.desc: Split a long list into multiple pages to browse, with a rows-per-page selector.
pagination.purpose: Let users move between pages when a list is too long to show all at once.
pagination.behavior: Pick a page number or click previous/next to move; you can change how many rows show per page.
pagination.avoid: A short list that fits fully on one page — pagination is not needed then.
pagination.when1: The end of a long table/list with many records
pagination.when2: Allowing the rows-per-page to be changed
pagination.do1: Set a sensible rows-per-page (10–50) so the page is not too long.
pagination.do2: Allow changing the rows-per-page for data tables with many records.
pagination.dont1: Paginating a very short list — users can see it all on one page.
pagination.exSizeD: A pagination bar placed below the content, with a selector for how many rows show per page so viewers can adjust it themselves.
pagination.exVarD: Three styles for quick reference: compact (current page number only), with a rows-per-page selector, and the full form with many page buttons.
pagination.exTableD: Pagination placed below a data table, slicing rows by page right there; the small, compact style for data-heavy screens.

anchor.title: Anchor
anchor.desc: A list of links that jump quickly to each section of a long page, marking the section being viewed.
anchor.purpose: Let users jump quickly to each section of a long page and always know which section they are on.
anchor.behavior: Clicking an item scrolls to the matching section; the item for the current section is highlighted automatically as you scroll.
anchor.avoid: A short page that fits neatly on one screen — no table of contents needed.
anchor.when1: A long employee-profile page split into several sections
anchor.when2: A document/policy that needs a quick-jump table of contents
anchor.when3: A page that needs to mark the current section while scrolling
anchor.do1: Use it for a long profile/document page split into clear sections.
anchor.do2: Keep item names short, matching the title of the section they point to.
anchor.do3: Pin the table of contents when the page is very long so users always see it and can switch sections.
anchor.dont1: Using it for a short page, or listing so many items that it becomes cluttered.
anchor.exVertD: A list of sections laid out vertically, usually placed in a column beside the content. Suits a long employee-profile page: General info, Contract, Salary, Allowances.
anchor.exHorizD: Sections laid out in a single horizontal row, placed at the top of the page as a compact navigation bar. Suits when there is no side column or the page is viewed on a wide screen.
anchor.exAffixD: The table of contents is pinned so it always shows as the user scrolls deep into a long profile page, helping them switch sections without scrolling back up.

pageHeader.title: Page Header
pageHeader.desc: The top of a detail page: back button, title, subtitle, status tag and the page's primary action buttons.
pageHeader.purpose: Show which profile/request the user is viewing and place the page's primary action buttons where they are easy to find.
pageHeader.behavior: The back button and title sit on the left, the status tag next to the title, and action buttons align to the right. You can add a breadcrumb above and a tab strip at the foot.
pageHeader.avoid: A list page or a page with no page-level actions — a section title is usually enough there.
pageHeader.when1: The top of an employee-profile detail screen
pageHeader.when2: The top of a request detail screen (leave, overtime)
pageHeader.when3: A page that needs a title, status and action buttons
pageHeader.do1: Place the primary action (Save/Approve) at the top right, level with the title, so users see it immediately.
pageHeader.do2: Use a status tag next to the title to summarize the record's state ("Active", "Pending approval").
pageHeader.do3: Add a back button when the page is opened from a list so users can return easily.
pageHeader.dont1: Cramming too many buttons into the header — keep only the 2-3 most important actions.
pageHeader.exDetailD: The top of an employee-profile screen: a back button to the list, a status tag next to the name, and the primary action buttons on the right.
pageHeader.exCrumbD: Add a breadcrumb above the title so users know the page's position in the system and can jump back to parent levels quickly.
pageHeader.exFooterD: Attach a tab strip to the foot of the header to switch between parts of the same profile — info, contract, attendance — without leaving the page.

tooltip.desc: A short explanatory line that appears when the user hovers over an element.
tooltip.purpose: Give a short explanation for a button or icon without taking up screen space.
tooltip.when2: Clarifying a technical term in a sentence
tooltip.behavior: Appears on hover or tap and hides itself when you move away.
tooltip.avoid: Long content or content that needs interaction — use a Popover instead.
tooltip.do1: Use it for icon-only buttons, with a concise one-line explanation.
tooltip.do2: Always label icon buttons so screen-reader users can read them.
tooltip.dont1: Putting important information only in a tooltip — it is hard to see on phones.
tooltip.exBarD: Each icon button on the action bar carries a one-line note telling what it does. It helps users recognize functions without text.
tooltip.exInlineT: Tooltip — Explaining a word in a sentence
tooltip.exInlineD: Hover over an underlined term in a paragraph to see a short definition. Use it to clarify a technical term right in place.
tooltip.inlinePost: at the start of each year.
tooltip.inlineTip: Unused leave days from the previous year carried over into this year
tooltip.exPlaceD: A tooltip can appear above, below, left or right of the element. Pick the direction with free space so the tooltip is not clipped by the screen.
tooltip.title: Tooltip

hoverCard.desc: Hover over an employee name or request code → a floating card summarizes the info for a quick look without leaving the page.
hoverCard.purpose: Answer 'who is this?' right in place — without making users open a profile screen.
hoverCard.when1: Employee names in tables and comments
hoverCard.when2: The approver on a request card
hoverCard.when3: A request or project code that needs a quick summary
hoverCard.behavior: Hover over the anchor element, wait ~0.15s and the card appears; move away and it closes itself. The screen supplies the card content via a template.
hoverCard.avoid: Long content or complex interactions — use a Drawer/Modal. Touch screens have no hover — provide another way to view the profile.
hoverCard.do1: Keep the card compact: avatar + name + 1-2 identifying lines + at most one button.
hoverCard.do2: Attach it to EVERY place a person's name appears (tables, comments, approvers) for consistent behavior.
hoverCard.dont1: Cramming a long table or list into the card — the card is only for a quick glance.
hoverCard.exProfileD: Hover over a name to see a mini profile: avatar, job title, department and a button to open the full profile.
hoverCard.title: Hover Card

commandPalette.desc: Press Ctrl/⌘+K anywhere: type a few characters to jump to a screen or run a command — no need to dig through menus.
commandPalette.purpose: A shortcut for power users: navigate + run actions from the keyboard, faster than digging through nested menus.
commandPalette.when2: Running an action you repeat many times a day
commandPalette.when3: Apps with many menus and keyboard-savvy users
commandPalette.behavior: Open with the shortcut or a button; type to filter by command name; ↑↓ to select, Enter to run, Esc to close. Permission-gated commands only appear for users who have that permission.
commandPalette.avoid: Replacing menus entirely — there must always be an equivalent mouse path.
commandPalette.do1: Place the component once in the shell; screens only register commands via the service.
commandPalette.do2: Group commands by context (Navigation, Create, Admin) — easy to scan when the list is long.
commandPalette.do3: Attach a perm to sensitive commands — do not expose commands a user has no permission to run.
commandPalette.dont1: Registering commands with duplicate functions — one command per task.
commandPalette.exTryD: This styleguide already has it wired up: click the button or press Ctrl/⌘+K, type 'table' or 'avatar' to jump to the matching page.
commandPalette.title: Command Palette

popover.desc: A small content panel that pops up next to an element, able to hold a title, rich content and even action buttons.
popover.ovContent: Detailed content shown in the popover when you click the button.
popover.purpose: Show secondary content (a long explanation, a quick profile, small actions) anchored next to an element without opening a full-screen dialog.
popover.when1: Quickly viewing a profile or secondary info
popover.when2: Gathering filters or options into a single button
popover.when3: A light confirmation right in place
popover.behavior: Pops up on click or hover over the button; can hold a title, rich content and buttons. Click outside to close.
popover.avoid: Just one line of explanation — use a Tooltip; heavy data entry — use a Dialog.
popover.do1: Keep the content focused on a single task or a single piece of information.
popover.do2: Always provide a clear way to close: click outside or a close/cancel button in the panel.
popover.dont1: Nesting a popover inside another popover — it becomes confusing to navigate.
popover.dont2: Cramming long scrollable content or a large form — use a dialog instead.
popover.exPlaceD: A popover can appear above, below, left or right of the element. Pick the direction with free space so the panel is not clipped by the screen edge.
popover.posTip: The popover follows the chosen direction.
popover.exProfileD: Hover over an employee name to see a condensed profile card: avatar, job title and status. It helps a quick lookup without leaving the page.
popover.exFilterD: A popover holding checkboxes to filter a list, plus Apply and Reset buttons. It gathers filters neatly in one place without taking up the data table's space.
popover.exConfirmD: Ask for confirmation right in place for a delete action, with Delete and Cancel buttons. It reminds users to think twice before an irreversible action.
popover.confirmBody: The profile will be removed from the list and cannot be restored.
popover.exSettingsD: A popover holding on/off switches to quickly adjust personal preferences like notifications and dark mode. Changes take effect immediately, no need to open a settings page.
popover.title: Popover

popconfirm.desc: A small box that pops up right next to the button, asking the user again before an irreversible action.
popconfirm.ovConfirm: Delete this employee? This action cannot be undone.
popconfirm.purpose: Ask the user to confirm a potentially destructive action before it runs — deleting data, revoking access, discarding unsaved changes.
popconfirm.when1: Deleting a row or a file in a table
popconfirm.when3: Any action that cannot be undone
popconfirm.behavior: Pops up right next to the button with a question + two choices, Confirm / Cancel. Choosing Cancel closes it and nothing changes.
popconfirm.avoid: Routine, non-destructive actions — just do them directly; do not force a needless confirmation that annoys users.
popconfirm.do1: Give the action button a specific label: "Delete contract" is clearer than "OK" or "Confirm".
popconfirm.do2: State the consequence in the question so users know what will happen before they click.
popconfirm.dont1: Using it for non-destructive actions — for routine tasks, use a normal button.
popconfirm.exDeleteD: A delete button asks again before it actually deletes. The Delete button is red to stress that this is an irreversible action.
popconfirm.delRowConfirm: Delete this row? It cannot be undone.
popconfirm.exLabelD: Change the text on the two buttons to match the real task. A specific label like 'Revoke access' lets users grasp the consequence at once, clearer than a generic 'OK'.
popconfirm.leaveConfirm: Leave the page? Unsaved changes will be lost.
popconfirm.exDangerD: Destructive actions use a red button; routine tasks (submit, approve) use a neutral button. Only go red when it is truly dangerous, so the warning does not lose its impact.
popconfirm.submitConfirm: Submit the leave request for your manager to approve?
popconfirm.exPlaceD: Pick the pop-up direction to suit the layout. A button at the top of a table can open downward, a button at the bottom of the page can open upward, avoiding covering important content.
popconfirm.title: Popconfirm

drawer.desc: A panel that slides in from the screen edge to view or edit an item's details without leaving the list page.
drawer.purpose: View or edit an item's details right next to the list, without switching to another page.
drawer.when1: Quick-viewing an item's details next to the list
drawer.when2: Quickly editing info without leaving the page
drawer.when3: Adding a new item with a short form
drawer.behavior: The panel slides in from a screen edge and dims the background behind it. Closing it returns you to the exact spot in the list.
drawer.avoid: Long, multi-step content that needs the whole screen — use a dedicated page instead of a narrow drawer.
drawer.do1: Use it to quick-view or quick-edit an item right next to the list.
drawer.do2: Give it a title that clearly names the item being worked on ("Employee profile", "Add department").
drawer.do3: For forms, open a wider drawer so fields are not cramped.
drawer.dont1: Cramming a long multi-step process into a narrow drawer.
drawer.exProfileD: Slide in from the right to quickly view an employee's info next to the list; when done, close it and you are back where you were. Suited for quick lookups.
drawer.exFormD: Put an input form in a wide drawer to add a new item without leaving the list. It has Save and Cancel buttons right inside the panel.
drawer.formBody: Fill in the new department's details then click Save.
drawer.exPlaceD: A drawer can slide in from the left, right, top or bottom. Right is the default for details; top/bottom suit filters or quick notifications.
drawer.bodyLeft: The panel enters from the left edge.
drawer.bodyRight: The panel enters from the right edge (default).
drawer.bodyTop: The panel enters from the top edge.
drawer.bodyBottom: The panel enters from the bottom edge.
drawer.exSizeD: Pick a width that fits the content: narrow for a quick glance at a few lines, medium for a full profile, wide for a form with many fields.
drawer.bodyNarrow: Enough for a few quick lines of info.
drawer.bodyWide: Wide for a form with many input fields.
drawer.title: Drawer

userCell.desc: Combines an avatar, a name and a secondary line (email/job title) into a compact cell for the employee column in a table.
userCell.purpose: Show an employee in a list table: who they are, plus secondary identifying details (email, job title).
userCell.behavior: Prefers a photo; without one, it shows initials colored by the name. The presence dot (if enabled) sits at the corner of the avatar. The name and secondary line truncate when the column is narrow.
userCell.avoid: Non-person data (companies, projects) — use the Media Cell for that.
userCell.do1: Always pass a name so initials appear when the image fails and screen readers can announce who it is.
userCell.do2: Put an email or job title on the secondary line to tell apart people with the same name.
userCell.dont1: Cramming too much text into the secondary line — keep it to one short identifying detail.
userCell.exFullD: The full two-line form. Use it for employee list tables when a profile photo and email are available. No presence dot.
userCell.exOneD: A condensed form for tables where each row has only one line of data: drop the secondary line and use a smaller avatar (28px) — shorter rows, faster scanning.
userCell.exInitialsD: When there is no photo, the initials take a color derived from the name (stable, distinguishes people). No extra configuration needed.
userCell.exStatusD: Only enable status for screens that need real-time work state: time tracking, online presence. List tables usually do NOT use it — off by default.
userCell.exManyD: Several user cells stacked like a real table column — one employee per row, no presence dot.
userCell.when1: The "Employee" column in a list table
userCell.when3: Anywhere you need photo + name + secondary details in one cell
userCell.title: User Cell

textCell.desc: Combines a primary line (bold) and a secondary line (muted) into a compact table cell — like a job title with tenure, or a code with a description.
textCell.purpose: Show two related pieces of information in one table cell: a prominent primary line and a secondary line that qualifies it.
textCell.behavior: The primary line is clearly bold; the secondary line is smaller and more muted right below it. You can add a leading icon to hint at the data type. Both lines truncate (with an ellipsis) when the column is narrow. Right-align cells that hold numbers.
textCell.avoid: An employee who has a profile photo — use the User Cell. Also don't cram in three or more lines or a whole paragraph.
textCell.do1: Put the most important information on the primary line and the qualifier on the secondary line (job title above, tenure below).
textCell.do2: Keep each line to one short piece — enough for readers to scan the whole column quickly.
textCell.do3: Right-align cells that hold numbers (salary, quantity, codes) for easier column comparison.
textCell.dont1: Writing a long sentence or two or three ideas on the secondary line — it will be clipped and hard to read.
textCell.dont2: Using it for a person's name with a profile photo — that's the User Cell's job.
textCell.exRoleD: The most common use: the primary line is the job position and the secondary line shows since when. Fits the 'Position' column in an employee list.
textCell.exCodeD: The primary line is an identifier code and the secondary line briefly explains what it is. Fits 'Employee code', 'Department code', 'Contract code' columns.
textCell.exIconD: Add an icon at the start of the cell to hint at the data type — job title, work location, identifier — helping readers recognize the column faster.
textCell.exNumD: Right-align so numbers line up down the column for easy scanning and comparison. Use it for salary, allowances, leave days, quantity.
textCell.when1: The "Position", "Employee code", "Department" columns in a table
textCell.when2: Anywhere you need a primary line with a qualifying secondary line
textCell.when3: Numeric columns that need right alignment (salary, quantity, codes)
textCell.title: Text Cell

mediaCell.desc: Combines a logo (or an icon) with a name and a secondary line into a compact cell for the company, project or asset column in a table.
mediaCell.purpose: Show a non-person entity — a company, project, department or asset — with a name and a secondary line of information, in a table cell.
mediaCell.behavior: Prefers a logo if available; without one, it shows a representative icon. The logo frame is square for projects and assets, and round for companies and brands. The name and secondary line truncate when the column is narrow.
mediaCell.avoid: A specific person (employee, candidate) — use the User Cell for that.
mediaCell.do1: Use this cell for companies, projects, departments and assets — things that are not people.
mediaCell.do2: Without a logo, pick an icon that fits the entity type: a folder for a project, a building for a company, a document for a contract.
mediaCell.do3: Keep the frame consistent within one table: if projects are square, every project row is square.
mediaCell.dont1: Using it for a person by dropping in a portrait photo — that's the User Cell's job.
mediaCell.dont2: Cramming a full address or long description into the secondary line — keep it to one short identifying detail.
mediaCell.exLogoD: The full form for a project row: logo, project name and member count. Use it for a project list table when a logo image is available.
mediaCell.exIconD: When a department or project has no logo of its own, pick a representative icon instead of an image. Viewers still recognize the type at a glance.
mediaCell.exShapeT: Square for projects, round for companies
mediaCell.exShapeD: A shape convention speeds classification: projects and assets use a square frame, while companies and brands use a round frame like a badge.
mediaCell.exManyD: Several media cells stacked like a real table column — one entity per row, with a consistent frame for easy scanning.
mediaCell.when1: The "Company", "Project" or "Department" column in a table
mediaCell.when3: Anywhere you need a logo/icon + name + secondary details in one cell
mediaCell.title: Media Cell

fileCell.desc: Shows an attached file in a table: a file-type icon, the file name and its size. The icon and color are derived from the file extension, so viewers instantly recognize a PDF, Word, Excel or image.
fileCell.purpose: Represent an attached file in a document list table: what the file is, its type and how large it is.
fileCell.behavior: The color and icon are inferred from the file extension — no configuration needed. The size shows on the secondary line under the name. Long file names truncate with an ellipsis when the column is narrow.
fileCell.avoid: Non-file data (person names, department names, status). For people use the User Cell, for status use the Status Cell.
fileCell.do1: Keep the real file name with its extension (e.g. ".pdf", ".xlsx") so the color and icon reflect the correct type.
fileCell.do2: Provide a pre-formatted size (e.g. "2.4 MB") so viewers can gauge the file weight before downloading.
fileCell.do3: If a file name has no extension, specify the file type so the cell still shows the right icon.
fileCell.dont1: Using an overly long file name with filler text — a narrow column will clip the important extension.
fileCell.dont2: Recoloring the icon to look "nicer" — the color here signifies the file type, so changing it arbitrarily is misleading.
fileCell.exTypesT: File types — a color for each
fileCell.exTypesD: The color and icon come from the file extension: PDF red, Word blue, Excel green, PowerPoint orange, archives (zip/rar) orange, images purple, everything else gray. Viewers tell document types apart at a glance.
fileCell.exSizeD: Add the size so viewers know how heavy a file is before downloading. The size line sits right under the file name.
fileCell.exNoExtD: When a file name is stored without an extension, specify the file type so the cell still shows the right icon and color — instead of falling back to the default gray icon.
fileCell.exListT: List of attachments in a profile
fileCell.exListD: Several file cells stacked like a real document column in an employee profile table — one file per row, a color per type, with sizes.
fileCell.rowNoExt: No extension → default gray · Type specified → correct color
fileCell.when1: The "Documents" / "Attachments" column in a profile table
fileCell.when3: Anywhere you need file type + name + size in one cell
fileCell.title: File Cell

statusCell.exSystemD: The 6 default system statuses from the State Machine diagram — use [preset] to auto-set the tone and label. Each status ships its standard action buttons (hrm-workflow-actions) matching the allowed transitions.
statusCell.desc: A compact cell that shows a row's status — working, on leave, pending… — through color and a label. A single component handles both the leading-dot style and the tinted-pill style, so you don't have to pick among different components.
statusCell.purpose: Quickly convey what state a row is in — through familiar color plus a text label — so viewers understand by scanning the column, without reading closely.
statusCell.behavior: Six color tones carry fixed meaning: green is good/complete, amber is needs attention, red is error/absent, blue is information, the 'processing' tone has a gently pulsing dot, and gray is neutral/stopped. The same status can appear in three styles: a dot with text, a tinted pill, or colored text only — choose by table density and how much emphasis you want.
statusCell.avoid: Don't use it to show people (names, employee photos) — that's the User Cell's job. This is only for statuses/classification labels.
statusCell.do1: Keep color meaning consistent across the system: green is always positive, red is always error/absent — users learn it once and rely on it in every table.
statusCell.do2: Within one column, pick a single display style (all dots, or all pills) so the column reads cleanly and lines up.
statusCell.do3: Keep labels short and use the right domain wording: "Working", "On leave", "Pending".
statusCell.do4: Use the STATUS component (hrm-status / hrm-status-cell) EVERYWHERE a tracked status is shown: table cell, card, detail drawer, header — not only inside a table cell.
statusCell.dont1: Relying on color alone to distinguish — always include a text label, because some people can't tell colors apart and printed color can shift.
statusCell.dont2: Assigning a contradictory color (e.g. red for a good status) just because it looks nice — color here carries meaning, it isn't decoration.
statusCell.dont3: Using a Tag to show a workflow status — Tag is for free-form labels/categories. A status (pending/approved/cancelled…) must use the Status component.
statusCell.exVariantsD: The same 'Working' status: Dot suits dense multi-row tables (subtle); Tinted pill with bold text — RECOMMENDED for process-status columns (prominent without looking like a button); Solid pill is easily mistaken for a button — use sparingly; Text only is the most compact. Same component, just a different variant.
statusCell.exFlowT: Process status — tinted pill + dot (badge, recommended)
statusCell.exFlowD: Tinted background + a small leading dot + semibold toned text: prominent enough to scan a table and see which step a request/profile is at, but not mistaken for a button like a solid background. The standard style for the key status column of an approval flow.
statusCell.exAttendD: A familiar status set for time-tracking / assignment tables. Each state has a fixed color so scanning the column makes it recognizable at once. 'Pending' has a gently pulsing dot hinting it's still awaiting action.
statusCell.exBadgeT: Order / record status column — pill style
statusCell.exBadgeD: The tinted-pill style fills the whole background with the tone color, standing out far more, and fits the key status column of an order or record. You can add a leading dot inside the pill for even stronger emphasis.
statusCell.exPaletteT: Six color tones and their meanings
statusCell.exPaletteD: The full palette for reference when choosing a tone for a new status. Colors adapt automatically to Light/Dark mode, no manual tweaking.
statusCell.rowVariants: Dot  ·  Tinted pill (recommended)  ·  Solid pill (limit)  ·  Text only
statusCell.rowPalette: Green  ·  Amber  ·  Red  ·  Blue  ·  Processing  ·  Neutral
statusCell.when1: The "Status" column in a list table
statusCell.when3: Status columns for orders, records, requests
statusCell.title: Status Cell

tagsCell.desc: Combines several classification tags (skills, departments, record types) into one cell; the overflow is collapsed into a “+N”.
tagsCell.purpose: Show a row's set of classification tags without breaking the column width.
tagsCell.behavior: Shows up to the allowed number of tags; the rest collapse into a single “+N” tag. Each tag can carry its own hue to distinguish groups.
tagsCell.avoid: Cramming dozens of tags into one cell — for a long list, show a few key tags then “+N”, and view details elsewhere.
tagsCell.do1: Limit visible tags to 2–3 to keep the column tidy; push the overflow into “+N”.
tagsCell.do2: Use a consistent hue for the same tag type (e.g. skills = blue, departments = purple).
tagsCell.dont1: Mixing too many vivid colors in one cell — it's cluttered and loses the classification meaning.
tagsCell.exSkillsD: A colored tag for each skill. Use it for the “Skills” column in an employee or candidate table.
tagsCell.exMaxD: Set a small maximum tag count; the overflow collapses. Keeps the column the same width even when a row has many tags.
tagsCell.exVariantD: The same tag set with different backgrounds: filled, light (the default), lighter, and stroke. Choose by how much prominence you want.
tagsCell.when2: When a row belongs to several classification groups
tagsCell.when3: You need to see a few key tags quickly, with overflow collapsed
tagsCell.title: Tags Cell

progressCell.desc: Represents a number against a maximum with a thin horizontal bar plus a percentage, compact in a table cell — so viewers grasp 'how far along' without reading the number.
progressCell.purpose: Show a row's completion or usage level: goal completion, training progress, storage used.
progressCell.behavior: The bar length is proportional to the value over the maximum (default 100). The percentage shows on the right (can be turned off). You can add a short label before the bar. Color is chosen by meaning; values above or below the range are clamped to 0–100%.
progressCell.avoid: Using it to compare several separate items side by side like a chart — this is only a single-row indicator, not a replacement for a bar chart.
progressCell.do1: Keep color meaning consistent across the table: the same red–amber–green convention for every row so the eye reads it instantly.
progressCell.do2: Show the percentage when the exact number matters (KPI, storage); hide it when you only need a quick sense of more-or-less.
progressCell.do3: Add a short label when the cell stands alone out of column context, so you know what the bar measures.
progressCell.dont1: Coloring just for decoration — color here should signify state (low/medium/high), otherwise leave it at the default.
progressCell.dont2: Putting a wordy label before the bar; a long label squeezes the bar too short to read.
progressCell.exGoalD: The same KPI column at different levels — the bar length shows at once who is near the finish and who is far off.
progressCell.exThresholdD: Use color to flag the level: red when still low, amber in the middle, green when high. Keep this convention the same across the column.
progressCell.exLabelD: Add a short label before the bar when the cell needs to explain itself: what it measures, how much is used. Fits rows for storage capacity and quotas.
progressCell.exBarD: Turn off the percentage when you only need a quick sense of more or less, or when the column is tight. The bar still conveys the level without adding a number.
progressCell.when1: The "Progress" / "Completion" column in KPI and goal tables
progressCell.when3: Showing storage usage or a quota in a single row
progressCell.title: Progress Cell

ratingCell.desc: Shows a rating as a row of stars in a table cell — compact and easy to compare across rows. View-only; users can't select a score here.
ratingCell.purpose: Quickly show a rating — competency, performance, satisfaction — as stars the eye reads at once, without reading a number.
ratingCell.behavior: Stars fill by the score and support half stars (e.g. 3.5 stars shows one star half-filled). You can add the score next to it for precise reading, and the number of ratings in parentheses like (128). This is a view-only cell — not a place for users to rate.
ratingCell.avoid: Using it where users need to give a score — this cell isn't selectable; use a rating input/control instead.
ratingCell.do1: Keep the same scale (usually 5 stars) across the column so rows can be compared with each other.
ratingCell.do2: Show the score when viewers need the exact number, for example to rank or reconcile.
ratingCell.do3: Add the rating count when trust matters — 4.5 stars from 200 ratings is more reliable than 5 stars from 2.
ratingCell.dont1: Using the star cell where users must give their own score — this cell is view-only.
ratingCell.dont2: Changing the maximum star count erratically between rows in the same table — viewers will misread it.
ratingCell.exLevelsD: The same 5-star scale at different levels. Half stars (4.5 and 2.5) show a star half-filled to reflect the fractional score accurately.
ratingCell.exValueD: Show the score for precise reading beside the star row. Fits when viewers need a concrete number rather than a visual estimate.
ratingCell.exCountD: Add the count in parentheses, e.g. (128), to show how many ratings the score is based on. Helps tell a trustworthy high score from a high score from too few ratings.
ratingCell.exColumnT: The 'Performance rating' column in an employee table
ratingCell.exColumnD: Several star cells stacked like a real table column — one employee per row. Use it for competency and periodic performance results or post-training feedback.
ratingCell.when1: The "Performance rating" or "Competency" column in an employee table
ratingCell.when2: Tables summarizing periodic review results, post-training feedback
ratingCell.when3: Anywhere you need to read a score quickly as stars rather than a bare number
ratingCell.title: Rating Cell

amountCell.desc: Shows a currency amount or quantity in a table: always right-aligned, with automatic thousands separators, a trailing unit and optional increase/decrease coloring — for payroll, allowance and bonus/penalty tables.
amountCell.purpose: Present a number — salary, allowance, bonus, penalty, hours or workdays — so the whole column lines up and is easy to scan and compare.
amountCell.behavior: The number always sits at the right edge with automatic thousands separators, so the digits line up down the column. The unit (₫, $, hours…) comes right after the number. When signed mode is on, positive numbers show a plus and turn green, negative show a minus and turn red, so you see increase or decrease at once. It rounds to a whole number by default; you can show decimals when needed.
amountCell.avoid: Text or non-numeric codes (names, job titles, record codes) — those should be left-aligned in a text cell. Also not for dates or status percentages.
amountCell.do1: Always right-align amounts so the whole column lines up, letting readers scan and add them up faster.
amountCell.do2: State the unit clearly (₫, hours, days) so no one has to guess what the number refers to.
amountCell.do3: Only enable the colored +/− for columns that truly signify increase/decrease, like bonus, penalty, difference.
amountCell.dont1: Left-aligning or centering amounts — the column becomes ragged and very hard to scan and compare.
amountCell.dont2: Coloring green/red for columns that are just ordinary numbers (base salary, hours) — color here must signify increase/decrease, not decoration.
amountCell.exSalaryD: The most common use in payroll tables: large amounts, automatic thousands separators, with the ₫ unit trailing. Fits 'Base salary', 'Allowance', 'Net pay' columns.
amountCell.exBonusD: Enable signed mode for columns that signify increase/decrease: positive shows a green plus (bonus, extra allowance), negative shows a red minus (penalty, deduction). One look tells you gain or loss.
amountCell.exHoursD: Not just money — use it for the numeric columns of a timesheet too. Change the unit to 'hours' or 'days', still right-aligned with thousands separators as usual.
amountCell.exDiffD: Combine colored signs with an hours or ₫ unit to make a comparison column: how much more (green) or less (red) this month is than last.
amountCell.when1: The "Salary", "Allowance", "Net pay" columns in a payroll table
amountCell.when2: The "Bonus", "Penalty", "Difference" columns that need clear increase/decrease
amountCell.when3: Columns of hours and workdays in a timesheet
amountCell.title: Amount Cell

trendCell.desc: Pairs a metric with an arrowed change so that, in a table, readers see at once whether it's rising, falling or flat — no mental comparison needed.
trendCell.purpose: Show how an HRM metric is moving versus the previous period: headcount, attendance rate, a KPI against last month.
trendCell.behavior: The sign and color follow the change: up shows a green up-arrow with a plus, down shows a red down-arrow with a minus, unchanged shows a gray dash. The main number comes first, the change after; you can hide the main number to leave just the arrow.
trendCell.avoid: Don't use it when you only need to show a static number (salary, balance) — that's the Amount Cell's job. The Trend Cell always implies 'versus an earlier baseline'.
trendCell.do1: Only use it when the number truly has a baseline to compare against — previous period, target, start of period — so the arrow means something.
trendCell.do2: Keep the same comparison baseline across the column (e.g. all "versus last month") so readers don't get confused.
trendCell.do3: Pick the right unit for what you measure: percent for rates, "people" for headcount, "hours" for duration.
trendCell.dont1: Coloring against meaning: a decrease isn't always bad (e.g. a lower turnover rate is good) — if the context could be misread, explain it clearly in the column header.
trendCell.dont2: Dropping a trend cell into a column where the number has no comparison baseline at all — the arrow will mislead.
trendCell.exPctD: The full and most common form: a number with a change measured in percent. Three colors for three directions — up (green), down (red), unchanged (gray) — let you grasp the trend by scanning the column.
trendCell.exDeltaOnlyD: Hide the main number, keep just the arrow and the change. Fits when the column already has the number elsewhere and here you only want to emphasize the direction, compactly.
trendCell.exUnitD: Change the unit of the delta to match what you measure. For example headcount rises/falls in 'people', overtime in 'hours' — instead of percent.
trendCell.exColumnT: A column in an HRM table
trendCell.exColumnD: Several trend cells stacked like a real column — e.g. 'Versus last month' for headcount metrics. Each row reads independently, but they share one comparison baseline, so scanning the column shows the overall picture.
trendCell.when1: The "Versus last month" / "Versus last period" column in a metrics table
trendCell.when2: Tables tracking headcount changes, attendance rate, overtime hours
trendCell.when3: Anywhere you need to see the up/down direction at once, not just the number
trendCell.title: Trend Cell

dateCell.desc: Shows a neatly formatted timestamp for a table column — date only, date with time, or time only — with an optional secondary line for a note.
dateCell.purpose: Present a timestamp in a table — hire date, contract signing date, clock-in time — in a consistent, readable format.
dateCell.behavior: Formats automatically: the date shows as day/month/year and the time as hour:minute. Choose the display mode: date only, date with time, or time only. The secondary line (if present) sits right below in smaller, muted text. Both lines stay on one row without wrapping midway.
dateCell.avoid: Using it to show a two-ended range (from date… to date…) in one cell — split it into two columns or two separate cells.
dateCell.do1: Use one consistent display mode across the column: either all date-only or all date-with-time — don't mix within the same column.
dateCell.do2: Only enable the time when it truly matters (time tracking, approval moment). For hire dates or contract dates, date only is tidier.
dateCell.do3: For a note like "3 days ago" or "yesterday", put that text into the secondary line yourself — this cell doesn't compute relative time.
dateCell.dont1: Expecting the cell to update "2 hours ago" to the correct figure as time passes — the secondary line is fixed text supplied by whoever prepares the data.
